periodic.intro: Almost everything in organic chemistry traces back to one question: how badly does a given atom want electrons? The periodic table answers that by position alone, which is why every exam hands you one and expects you to reason from it.

sections.heading: Why the table is arranged this way
body: Elements are laid out by atomic number — the number of protons. That ordering isn't arbitrary bookkeeping: it produces columns of elements that behave almost identically, because behaviour is set by the outermost electrons, and elements in a column have the same number of them.

Those outermost electrons are the valence electrons, and they are the only ones that do chemistry. Carbon's inner pair never participates in a reaction. Its four valence electrons do all the work. This is why the column an element sits in predicts its chemistry so reliably.

example.label: Reading valence off the table
example.text: Groups 1 and 2 have 1 and 2 valence electrons. For groups 13–18, subtract 10 from the group number: group 16 (oxygen) has 6, group 17 (halogens) has 7. Oxygen needs 2 more to reach 8, so it forms 2 bonds. Halogens need 1, so they form 1.

sections.heading: Shells, and why the octet is eight
body: Electrons occupy shells numbered outward from the nucleus, and each shell holds a fixed maximum: 2n², where n is the shell number. So shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 18, shell 4 holds 32.

Shells are divided into subshells of different shapes. An s subshell is one orbital holding 2 electrons. A p subshell is three orbitals holding 6. A d subshell is five orbitals holding 10, and f is seven holding 14. Each orbital takes exactly two electrons, so the capacities are just the orbital counts doubled.

This is where the octet rule comes from. It is not a separate fact to memorize: the second shell contains one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals, total capacity 8. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine all have the second shell as their valence shell, so a full valence shell for them means eight electrons. Hydrogen has only the first shell, capacity 2, which is why it wants a duet instead.

example.label: Why sulfur breaks the rule and nitrogen cannot
example.text: Sulfur is in shell 3, which includes d orbitals and so has room beyond 8 — hence SF₆. Nitrogen is in shell 2, which has only s and p and caps at 8 permanently. There is no NF₅.

sections.heading: Filling order, without memorizing a list
body: Electrons fill from lowest energy upward, but subshell energies overlap between shells — the 4s actually sits below the 3d, so it fills first even though its shell number is higher. Filling order is therefore not simply 1s, 2s, 3s.

Rather than memorizing nineteen items in sequence, use the diagonal rule. Write the subshells in rows by shell number — 1s / 2s 2p / 3s 3p 3d / 4s 4p 4d 4f — then read the diagonals from top-right down to bottom-left. The order falls out of the geometry: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s.

For organic chemistry the practical answer is much shorter. Everything you meet has its valence electrons in the first three shells, so you rarely need past 3p. Carbon is 1s² 2s² 2p². The full chart matters for transition metals and gen-chem exams.

example.label: Reading a configuration back
example.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ — the highest shell present is 3, holding 2 + 5 = 7 valence electrons. Seven valence electrons means group 17, and 17 total electrons means chlorine.

sections.heading: Electronegativity: the pull on shared electrons
body: When two atoms share a pair of electrons, they rarely share equally. Electronegativity measures how hard an atom pulls on that shared pair. Fluorine pulls hardest of all elements; the metals at the bottom left pull least.

Two forces set it. Moving right across a row, protons pile up in the nucleus while electrons go into the same shell — more positive charge, same distance, so the pull rises. Moving down a column, each row adds a whole new shell, so the valence electrons sit further out and are shielded by the ones beneath. Distance wins, and the pull drops.
Combine those and you get the rule you'll use constantly: electronegativity increases up and to the right.

sections.heading: When 'up and to the right' isn't enough
body: That rule only settles a comparison along one axis. If two elements are in the same row, compare across. Same column, compare down. But if they differ in both — a diagonal pair — the two halves of the rule point opposite ways and it answers nothing.

For those, fall back on something simpler and more reliable: metals versus nonmetals. Metals hold their outer electrons loosely; nonmetals grip them tightly. Every nonmetal is more electronegative than every metal, with no exceptions worth worrying about.

example.label: Lithium vs iodine
example.text: Lithium is up (favouring Li) but far left (favouring I). The trend deadlocks. But lithium is a metal and iodine is a nonmetal, so iodine wins — 2.66 against 0.98. No numbers needed to get there.

sections.heading: The ten elements that actually matter
body: Organic chemistry runs almost entirely on C, H, N, O, plus the halogens F, Cl, Br, I, plus S and P. Everything else appears as a reagent, not as part of the molecule.

For those ten, the bonding pattern is worth knowing cold, because you'll use it every time you check whether a structure is drawn correctly: carbon makes 4 bonds, nitrogen 3, oxygen 2, and hydrogen and the halogens 1 each. Sulfur behaves like oxygen (2), phosphorus like nitrogen (3).

polarity.intro: Reactions happen where charge is uneven. Before you can predict where a molecule reacts, you need to see which atoms are electron-rich and which are electron-poor — and that comes almost entirely from comparing electronegativities.

sections.heading: Three kinds of bond, decided by position
body: Start with the question that needs no numbers: is each atom a metal or a nonmetal? A metal bonded to a nonmetal transfers electrons outright and you get an ionic bond — a lattice of separate ions, like table salt. Two nonmetals share instead, giving a covalent bond. Two metals pool their electrons into a 'sea', which is metallic bonding.
This is the rule to reach for first, because a periodic table is the one reference every exam supplies, while electronegativity values are printed on none of them.

example.label: Two quick calls
example.text: K–Br: potassium is a metal, bromine a nonmetal → ionic. C–O: both nonmetals → covalent. Neither answer needed a number.

sections.heading: Polar or nonpolar — the second question
body: Once you know a bond is covalent, ask whether the sharing is even. Two identical atoms share perfectly evenly: nonpolar. Two different atoms don't, and the more electronegative one takes a larger share of the electron density.

That atom picks up a partial negative charge, written δ−. Its partner is left partially positive, δ+. These are partial charges, not full ones — nobody has gained or lost an electron, the pair is just sitting closer to one end.

sections.heading: Why any of this matters
body: The δ+ atom is electron-poor, and electron-rich species are attracted to it. That is the single most useful thing bond polarity tells you: it marks where a molecule will be attacked.

A carbon bonded to oxygen or a halogen is δ+, which is why those carbons are the reactive ones in nearly every mechanism you'll see. A carbon bonded only to hydrogen and other carbons is essentially neutral, which is why hydrocarbon chains just sit there being unreactive.

example.label: The C–H exception worth internalizing
example.text: Carbon is 2.55 and hydrogen 2.20 — close enough that C–H counts as effectively nonpolar. This is why oils and fats don't dissolve in water, and why the hydrocarbon parts of a molecule hide from it.

sections.heading: A whole molecule can be nonpolar even with polar bonds
body: Bond polarity and molecular polarity are different questions. Each polar bond has a direction, and those directions can cancel if the molecule is symmetric enough.

Carbon tetrachloride has four strongly polar C–Cl bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. They pull equally in opposing directions and cancel exactly, so the molecule has no net dipole at all. Break the symmetry — swap one chlorine for a hydrogen — and the cancellation fails, leaving chloroform distinctly polar.
Two things break symmetry: a lone pair on the central atom (which is why water is bent and polar), or outer atoms that aren't all the same.

lewis.intro: A Lewis structure is a bookkeeping system for valence electrons. Getting fluent at drawing and reading them matters because every mechanism you'll ever push arrows through is drawn on top of one.

sections.heading: What the drawing represents
body: Every line between two atoms is a shared pair of electrons — one bond, two electrons. Every pair of dots sitting on a single atom is a lone pair: two electrons that belong to that atom alone and aren't being shared.

Lone pairs are not decoration. They are where most reactions start, because an atom with an available pair is an atom that can attack something. Leaving them off a drawing hides the reactive part of the molecule.

sections.heading: The octet rule, and what it really says
body: Most second-row atoms are stable with eight electrons around them, counting both bonding and lone pairs. That's not a law of nature so much as a consequence of shell capacity: the second shell holds exactly eight (one s orbital plus three p orbitals, two electrons each).
Hydrogen is the exception everyone forgets — it only has a first shell, which holds two. Hydrogen wants a duet, not an octet.
There are real exceptions beyond that. Boron is commonly stable with only six. Elements from the third row down (S, P, Cl) can exceed eight, because they have d orbitals available.

sections.heading: Building one, step by step
body: Count all the valence electrons first, adding one for each negative charge and subtracting one for each positive charge. That total is your budget — every electron has to end up somewhere.

Connect the atoms with single bonds, then hand out remaining electrons as lone pairs to the outer atoms until they have octets. If the central atom is short, pull a lone pair from a neighbour into a second bond. You're rearranging, never adding.

example.label: Water, worked
example.text: Oxygen brings 6, each hydrogen brings 1: 8 electrons total. Two O–H bonds use 4. The remaining 4 become two lone pairs on oxygen. Oxygen now has 8 around it, each hydrogen has its duet, and the whole budget is spent.

sections.heading: Formal charge: who owns what
body: Formal charge asks whether an atom is holding its fair share of electrons. Take its normal valence count, subtract the lone-pair electrons it keeps entirely, and subtract half of the shared ones.
In practice it's faster as: valence − lone pair electrons − number of bonds. An oxygen with two bonds and two lone pairs gives 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, which is why that's oxygen's neutral, happy arrangement.

Learn the neutral patterns and you can spot charges instantly instead of computing them: carbon with 4 bonds, nitrogen with 3 bonds and a lone pair, oxygen with 2 bonds and two lone pairs. Deviate from those and there's a charge.

example.label: Spotting charges by pattern
example.text: Nitrogen with 4 bonds is one more than neutral → +1 (ammonium). Oxygen with 3 bonds is one more than neutral → +1. Oxygen with 1 bond and 3 lone pairs is one fewer → −1 (hydroxide).

vsepr.intro: Molecules are three-dimensional, and their shape decides how they pack, whether they're polar, and how reagents can approach them. VSEPR is a surprisingly simple way to predict that shape from a flat drawing.

sections.heading: The whole idea in one sentence
body: Electron groups around an atom repel each other, so they spread out as far apart as they can get. That's it. Everything else is working out the geometry that maximizes separation for a given number of groups.

The crucial move is counting GROUPS, not bonds. An electron group is any single, double, or triple bond, or any lone pair. A double bond counts as one group, not two — both pairs sit between the same two atoms and point the same direction.

sections.heading: Groups to shape
body: Two groups get as far apart as possible by pointing in opposite directions: 180°, linear. Three spread into a flat triangle: 120°, trigonal planar. Four can't stay flat and still be maximally separated, so they pyramid out into three dimensions: 109.5°, tetrahedral.
Hybridization follows straight from the same count, with no extra work: 2 groups is sp, 3 is sp², 4 is sp³. The number in the label is literally how many p orbitals got mixed in.

example.label: CO₂ catches people out
example.text: Carbon has two double bonds and no lone pairs. Two groups, not four — so CO₂ is linear at 180°, and because it's symmetric, nonpolar despite two strongly polar bonds.

sections.heading: Electron geometry versus molecular shape
body: Here's where most mistakes happen. Electron geometry describes where all the groups point, lone pairs included. Molecular shape describes only where the ATOMS are — you can't see a lone pair.

Water has four groups, so its electron geometry is tetrahedral. But two of those groups are lone pairs, and the remaining atoms form a bent shape. Both descriptions are true; they answer different questions.

Lone pairs also squeeze the angles. They're held closer to the nucleus and take up more angular room than a bonding pair, so each one pushes the remaining bonds slightly closer together. Methane sits at the ideal 109.5°, ammonia (one lone pair) at about 107°, water (two) at about 104.5°.

sections.heading: Sigma and pi, and why rotation matters
body: A single bond is one sigma bond, formed by orbitals overlapping head-on along the axis between the atoms. That overlap is unchanged if you spin one end, which is why single bonds rotate freely at room temperature.

A double bond is one sigma plus one pi. The pi bond comes from two p orbitals overlapping sideways, above and below the axis. Rotating one end would tear that overlap apart, so double bonds are locked.
That locking is the entire reason cis and trans isomers exist — and why an alkene is a rigid, flat piece of a molecule while an alkane chain flops around freely.

imf.intro: Intermolecular forces are the attractions BETWEEN molecules, and they explain the properties you can actually observe: what melts, what boils, what dissolves in what. Every extraction and purification you'll do in lab is this reasoning applied.

sections.heading: Between, not within
body: This distinction is worth being pedantic about. Covalent bonds hold a molecule together internally. Intermolecular forces hold separate molecules near each other. The second kind are roughly ten to a hundred times weaker.

So when water boils, the hydrogen bonds between molecules break and the molecules fly apart — but each H₂O survives intact. If boiling broke covalent bonds, steam would be hydrogen and oxygen gas. Phase changes are always about intermolecular forces.

sections.heading: The three forces, weakest first
body: London dispersion is present in every molecule without exception. Electrons are constantly moving, so at any instant they're slightly lopsided, creating a fleeting dipole that induces one in the neighbour. Individually feeble, but it scales with size and surface contact — and in a large molecule it dominates everything else.
Dipole-dipole attraction appears in any polar molecule: the δ+ end of one is drawn to the δ− end of the next. Stronger than dispersion at comparable size.

Hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the three, but it's fussy about requirements. It needs a hydrogen bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine on one molecule, and a lone pair on N, O, or F on the other. A C–H hydrogen does not qualify, however polar the rest of the molecule.

sections.heading: Donors and acceptors
body: It helps to split hydrogen bonding into two roles. A donor supplies the hydrogen — it needs an actual H attached to N, O, or F. An acceptor supplies a lone pair for someone else's hydrogen.
An alcohol does both: its O–H donates, its oxygen lone pairs accept. An ether has the lone pairs but no O–H, so it can only accept. That single difference is worth about 80°C of boiling point.

example.label: Same formula, very different behaviour
example.text: Butan-1-ol and diethyl ether are both C₄H₁₀O. The alcohol boils at 118°C, the ether at 35°C. Identical size, identical mass — the gap is almost entirely the ability to donate a hydrogen bond.

sections.heading: Predicting boiling points
body: Work in this order. First compare size: bigger molecules have more dispersion, and if the sizes differ a lot that can settle it on its own. If sizes are comparable, ask which strongest force each molecule can use.

Shape matters too, at equal size. A straight chain packs closely against its neighbours and maximizes contact; a branched isomer is more spherical and touches less, so it boils lower. Pentane boils at 36°C, its fully branched isomer neopentane at 10°C — same formula, same mass, less contact.

sections.heading: Like dissolves like
body: For something to dissolve, the new solute-solvent attractions have to compensate for the solvent-solvent attractions being broken. Water molecules hold each other with strong hydrogen bonds, and a nonpolar solute offers nothing comparable in return — so it doesn't dissolve.

This is why alcohols with short chains mix freely with water while long-chain ones don't: the O–H head can hydrogen bond, but past four or five carbons the hydrocarbon tail dominates and the molecule behaves like an oil.

acidbase.intro: Acid-base chemistry is the most reused idea in organic chemistry. Most mechanisms begin or end with a proton moving, and the reasoning that predicts acid strength is the same reasoning that predicts stability, reactivity, and leaving-group ability.

sections.heading: Two definitions, both useful
body: The Brønsted-Lowry definition is about protons: an acid donates H⁺, a base accepts it. This is the one to use when something obviously gains or loses a hydrogen.

The Lewis definition is broader and about electrons: an acid accepts an electron pair, a base donates one. This turns out to be the more useful lens for mechanisms, because it covers reactions where no proton moves at all. Every nucleophile is a Lewis base; every electrophile is a Lewis acid.

sections.heading: pKa, and why lower means stronger
body: pKa is a logarithmic measure of how readily an acid gives up its proton. Lower means stronger, and because it's a log scale, each unit is a factor of ten. A pKa difference of 11 between acetic acid and ethanol is a factor of a hundred billion.

The values are worth anchoring roughly rather than precisely: strong mineral acids sit below zero, carboxylic acids around 5, ammonium around 10, water at 15.7, alcohols around 16, and C–H bonds are so weakly acidic they run from 25 up to 50.

sections.heading: The one rule for reaction direction
body: An acid-base reaction always favours the side with the WEAKER acid — the higher pKa. That's it. If you can identify the acid on each side and compare their pKa values, you know which way the equilibrium sits.

This is enormously practical. It tells you whether a given base is strong enough to deprotonate a given compound, which is the first thing you need to know before drawing any mechanism that starts with deprotonation.

example.label: Will hydroxide deprotonate a carboxylic acid?
example.text: The acid on the left is the carboxylic acid, pKa 4.8. If hydroxide takes the proton, the acid on the right is water, pKa 15.7. Products hold the weaker acid, so yes — and by about eleven orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Predicting acid strength: always look at the conjugate base
body: Acidity is really a question about what's left behind. If the anion formed by losing the proton is stable, the acid gives it up readily. If that anion is a miserable, high-energy species, the acid holds on.
So the habit to build is: deprotonate both compounds first, draw both anions, then ask which is more stable. Comparing the acids directly will mislead you.
Four factors decide it, and they're checked in a fixed order because earlier ones dominate later ones — remembered as ARIO.

sections.heading: ARIO in order
body: ATOM comes first and is by far the largest effect. If the charges sit on different atoms, that usually settles it. Across a row, more electronegative atoms hold negative charge better (O beats N beats C). Down a column, bigger wins instead, because the charge spreads over more volume (S beats O, I beats Cl).
RESONANCE is next. If the atoms tie, ask whether either anion can spread its charge over several atoms. A carboxylate spreads its charge over two oxygens; an alkoxide can't spread it at all.
INDUCTION follows. Electronegative atoms nearby pull electron density away through the sigma bonds, stabilizing the charge. The effect falls off sharply with distance.

ORBITAL is last and weakest. More s-character holds a lone pair closer to the nucleus, so sp beats sp² beats sp³. It only matters when everything else has tied — which is exactly the case for alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.

example.label: Stopping at the first difference
example.text: Ethanol vs acetic acid: both put the charge on oxygen, so ATOM ties. Move to RESONANCE — the carboxylate delocalizes, the alkoxide doesn't. Acetic acid is the stronger acid, and you never need to check induction or orbital.

aminoacids.intro: Biochemistry treats the twenty amino acids as vocabulary from the first lecture and never slows down for them again. Learning them properly beforehand is the single highest-return thing you can do for that course.

sections.heading: One skeleton, twenty side chains
body: Every amino acid is built on the same small frame: a central carbon with four things attached. Two of those are the groups the name comes from — an AMINO group and a CARBOXYL group — plus a hydrogen, plus one variable group written R.
The amino group is –NH₂: a nitrogen carrying two hydrogens. Nitrogen has a spare lone pair, so it readily picks up a proton and becomes –NH₃⁺.

The carboxyl group is –COOH: a carbon double bonded to one oxygen and single bonded to an –OH. That hydroxyl hydrogen comes off easily, leaving –COO⁻. This is the acidic end, and it is where "amino acid" gets its second word.
That frame is identical in nineteen of the twenty. Only R changes. Proline is the exception — its side chain loops back and bonds to the backbone nitrogen, which locks its geometry.
So learning the amino acids means learning twenty side chains, not twenty molecules. The Notes tab has all twenty drawn out, browsable and as flashcards.

example.label: Reading the name off the structure
example.text: Amino (–NH₂) + acid (–COOH) on the same carbon = amino acid. Everything that distinguishes one from another hangs below that carbon as R.

sections.heading: Why they're drawn charged
body: At physiological pH, the carboxyl group has given up its proton (becoming −COO⁻) and the amino group has picked one up (becoming −NH₃⁺). The molecule carries both a positive and a negative charge while being neutral overall — a zwitterion.
This isn't a technicality. It's why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points rather than oily liquids: they behave like salts.

sections.heading: Sorting them into five groups
body: Rather than memorizing twenty facts, sort by what the side chain contains. If it's a carboxylic acid, the residue is ACIDIC — that's only aspartate and glutamate. If it contains an amine, guanidinium, or imidazole, it's BASIC — only lysine, arginine, and histidine.

That's five residues carrying charge. Everything else is neutral, split into POLAR (containing an −OH, −SH, or amide: serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine, asparagine, glutamine) and NONPOLAR (pure hydrocarbon or an aromatic ring with nothing polar on it).
Learn the charged five and the rest follows by elimination.

example.label: The amide trap
example.text: Asparagine and glutamine are the amide versions of aspartate and glutamate. Amides are NEUTRAL. Confusing them with the acids is one of the most common early biochem mistakes.

sections.heading: The side-chain vocabulary you need
body: Sorting the twenty is much easier once you can name what is hanging off them, and only a handful of groups appear.

A HYDROXYL (–OH) makes a residue polar: serine, threonine, tyrosine. A THIOL (–SH) is the sulfur version, in cysteine, more acidic and far more reactive. An AMIDE (–CONH₂) is a carbonyl bonded to a nitrogen and is NEUTRAL — asparagine and glutamine, which is the trap, since they look like the acids.
A CARBOXYL (–COOH) is what makes aspartate and glutamate acidic. An AMINE, a GUANIDINIUM, or an IMIDAZOLE ring makes lysine, arginine and histidine basic.
Everything else is either a plain hydrocarbon or an aromatic ring with nothing polar attached, and those are the nonpolar ones that bury themselves inside a folded protein.

example.label: The amide trap, concretely
example.text: Aspartate ends in –COOH and is negative at pH 7.4. Asparagine ends in –CONH₂ and is neutral. One oxygen swapped for a nitrogen changes the charge entirely, and the names differ by two letters.

sections.heading: Side-chain pKa: which are actually charged
body: Seven side chains can gain or lose a proton, and their pKa values tell you what they look like at physiological pH 7.4. Compare the pKa to the pH: below its pKa a group keeps its proton, above it the proton is gone.
Aspartate (3.9) and glutamate (4.3) are well below 7.4, so they're deprotonated and negative. Lysine (10.5) and arginine (12.5) are well above, so they're protonated and positive.

Histidine sits at 6.0 — close enough to physiological pH that it can be either. That's what makes it uniquely useful in enzyme active sites: it can pick up or hand off a proton under normal cellular conditions, which is exactly what acid-base catalysis requires.

sections.heading: The handful with special jobs
body: A few residues carry outsized importance and are worth knowing individually. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen, making it the only achiral amino acid and the most conformationally flexible.

Proline's ring locks its geometry, so it breaks alpha helices. Cysteine's thiol can oxidize with another cysteine to form a disulfide bridge — the only covalent crosslink holding a folded protein together. Methionine always starts a newly translated protein, since AUG is the start codon.

buffers.intro: Biochemistry asks constantly whether a group is protonated, because that determines its charge, and charge determines whether an enzyme works. All of it reduces to comparing two numbers: the pH and the pKa.

sections.heading: The comparison that answers everything
body: A group's pKa is the pH at which it's exactly half protonated. Below that pH, it mostly holds its proton. Above it, the proton is mostly gone. That's the whole rule.
But knowing whether a group is protonated is only half the answer — you then have to ask what that means for CHARGE, and it depends on what kind of group it is.
A neutral acid like −COOH becomes −COO⁻ when deprotonated: neutral to negative. A positive amine like −NH₃⁺ becomes −NH₂: positive to neutral. Same event, opposite consequences.

example.label: Two side chains at pH 7.4
example.text: Aspartate, pKa 3.9: pH is above, so deprotonated, so −COO⁻ and negative. Lysine, pKa 10.5: pH is below, so protonated, so −NH₃⁺ and positive.

sections.heading: Henderson-Hasselbalch, and what it's really saying
body: The equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) looks intimidating and says something simple: the further the pH sits above the pKa, the more of the deprotonated form you have — logarithmically.

At pH = pKa, the log term is zero and the two forms are present in equal amounts. One unit above, the ratio is 10:1 in favour of the base form. Two units above, 100:1. Below the pKa it runs the other way.
In practice you rarely need to calculate anything. You need to know which side of the pKa you're on, and roughly how lopsided that makes things.

sections.heading: What makes a buffer work
body: A buffer resists pH change because it contains meaningful amounts of both a weak acid and its conjugate base. Add acid, and the base form absorbs it. Add base, and the acid form neutralizes it.

That only works while both forms are actually present, which is why the useful buffering range is roughly pKa ± 1. Beyond that one form runs out and the buffer stops buffering. Buffering is strongest exactly at pH = pKa, where the two forms are equal.
So choosing a buffer is simple: pick the one whose pKa is closest to the pH you want to hold. Phosphate (7.2) and HEPES (7.5) are the standards for biological work near 7.4.

sections.heading: Isoelectric point
body: The pI is the pH at which a molecule carries no NET charge — positive and negative contributions exactly cancel. For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, it's the average of the two pKa values flanking the neutral form.

It's worth knowing because proteins are least soluble at their pI. With no net charge, molecules stop repelling each other and clump together, which is the basis of isoelectric precipitation and of separating proteins by isoelectric focusing.

skeletal.intro: Organic chemists stopped drawing every carbon and hydrogen a long time ago, because molecules got too big for it. Line-angle structures are the shorthand that replaced it, and lectures are drawn in it from the first week. If reading one takes conscious effort, you spend your attention decoding notation instead of following chemistry.

sections.heading: The convention
body: Every corner and every free line end is a carbon atom. Nothing is written for them — the vertex IS the carbon.

Hydrogens attached to carbon are invisible too. You infer them: carbon always forms exactly four bonds, so however many bonds you can see, the rest are hydrogens. A vertex with two lines drawn to it has two hydrogens.

Everything that is not carbon or a carbon-bound hydrogen does get written out. Oxygens, nitrogens, halogens, and any hydrogen attached to those atoms all appear explicitly, because those are the reactive parts.

example.label: Why the hydrogens are hidden
example.text: Cholesterol has 46 hydrogens. Drawing each one would bury the four rings and the one hydroxyl group that actually determine how it behaves. Hiding them is not laziness — it is emphasis.

sections.heading: Counting hydrogens on any carbon
body: Subtract the bonds you can see from four. A chain-end carbon shows one bond, so it carries three hydrogens. A carbon in the middle of a chain shows two, so it carries two.
Count bonds, not neighbours: a double bond counts as two. A carbon with a double bond and one single bond shows three bonds, so it has one hydrogen.

sections.heading: Degrees of unsaturation
body: A saturated chain of n carbons holds 2n+2 hydrogens — the maximum possible. Every ring and every pi bond costs you two hydrogens against that maximum.
So comparing a molecular formula to the saturated maximum tells you how many rings plus pi bonds it must contain, before you have drawn anything. That number is the degrees of unsaturation.
Four degrees is worth recognizing on sight: it usually signals a benzene ring, which is one ring plus three double bonds.

example.label: Working it out for benzene
example.text: C6H6. A saturated six-carbon chain would hold 2(6)+2 = 14 hydrogens. It has 6, a shortfall of 8, which is 4 pairs — so 4 degrees of unsaturation. One ring plus three double bonds accounts for exactly that.

sections.heading: Why fluency here pays off more than anything else
body: This is the least intellectually demanding topic in the course and the highest-leverage one to over-practise. It is pure pattern recognition, and it becomes automatic with repetition.

Every later topic assumes it. Mechanisms, spectroscopy, stereochemistry — all of them are drawn in this notation, and any effort you are still spending on decoding is effort not spent on the actual chemistry.

functional.intro: Organic chemistry would be unmanageable if every molecule behaved uniquely. It is manageable because reactivity is concentrated in small recurring clusters of atoms — functional groups — and a molecule containing a given group behaves much like every other molecule containing it.

sections.heading: The organizing idea
body: A functional group is a specific arrangement of atoms that reacts in a characteristic way. The hydrocarbon skeleton around it is largely inert scaffolding.

This is why a course can cover millions of compounds in a semester. You are not learning molecules; you are learning perhaps fifteen groups and how each behaves. Ethanol and hexadecanol differ enormously in size but share an alcohol group and undergo the same reactions at it.

sections.heading: Why the groups are reactive
body: Nearly every functional group contains an electronegative atom — oxygen, nitrogen, a halogen — or a pi bond. Both create the uneven electron distribution that reactions require.

An electronegative atom pulls density away from its carbon, leaving that carbon electron-poor and open to attack. A pi bond does the opposite: its electrons are loosely held and exposed, so the pi bond itself attacks electron-poor things.
So identifying the functional group tells you where the molecule reacts and, usually, in which direction the electrons will flow.

sections.heading: The carbonyl family
body: A carbon double-bonded to oxygen — the carbonyl — is the single most important group in the course, and several groups are just a carbonyl with different neighbours.
Carbonyl with two carbons attached is a ketone. With a hydrogen on one side, an aldehyde. Add an −OH and it becomes a carboxylic acid; an −OR gives an ester; an −NR2 gives an amide.

Learning them as one family with variations is far easier than as five separate facts, and it predicts their behaviour: all of them have the same electron-poor carbonyl carbon, modified by whatever is attached.

example.label: Alcohol versus ether
example.text: An alcohol is R−OH; an ether is R−O−R. One difference — whether the oxygen carries a hydrogen — and it changes the boiling point by about 80 degrees, because only the alcohol can donate a hydrogen bond.

sections.heading: How to identify them quickly
body: Scan for the non-carbon atoms first. In a line-angle drawing they are the only things written out, so they are visually obvious, and they mark where every functional group is.

Then check what each is attached to. An oxygen with one bond to carbon and one to hydrogen is an alcohol; an oxygen bridging two carbons is an ether; an oxygen double-bonded to carbon is some kind of carbonyl, and its neighbours tell you which.

nomenclature.intro: IUPAC naming is a system for turning a structure into a unique name and back. It looks like arbitrary rule-following, but it is really a small, consistent grammar, and you only need a fraction of it to handle everything an introductory course throws at you.

sections.heading: Three pieces to every name
body: A name has a root telling you the longest carbon chain, a suffix telling you the principal functional group, and prefixes listing everything else hanging off it.
The roots are worth memorizing outright, because everything else is built on them: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6), hept (7), oct (8), non (9), dec (10).
So hexanol is a six-carbon chain (hex) that is an alcohol (-ol), and 2-chlorobutane is a four-carbon chain (but) with a chlorine on the second carbon.

sections.heading: Finding the parent chain
body: The parent is the LONGEST continuous chain of carbons — and it does not have to be the one drawn horizontally. Molecules are often drawn so the longest chain turns a corner, which is a deliberate test of whether you are counting rather than eyeballing.
If two chains tie in length, choose the one with more substituents attached.

sections.heading: Numbering, and the lowest-locant rule
body: Number the parent chain from whichever end gives the substituents the lowest possible numbers. Compare the full set of numbers, not just the first one, and pick the lower set.
A functional group suffix outranks substituents: if the chain contains an −OH, that gets the lowest number available regardless of where the halogens fall.

example.label: Which end to count from
example.text: A five-carbon chain with a chlorine on the second carbon from the left. Counting from the left gives locant 2; from the right it gives 4. Lower wins, so it is 2-chloropentane, never 4-chloropentane.

sections.heading: Assembling the name
body: List substituents alphabetically, each with its locant. When a substituent appears more than once, use di, tri, or tetra — but ignore those multiplying prefixes when alphabetizing. Diethyl files under E, not D.

A common early error is naming a substituent that should have been part of the parent chain. If you find yourself writing "1-methyl" anything, stop: a methyl on carbon 1 just means the chain was one carbon longer than you counted.

isomers.intro: Two compounds can share a molecular formula and still be completely different substances. Sorting out how they differ is the groundwork for stereochemistry, which is where a lot of students first get lost — largely because the vocabulary arrives faster than the ideas.

sections.heading: A decision tree, not a list
body: Start with the formula. If two molecules have different molecular formulas, they are simply different compounds and not isomers at all.
Same formula, different connectivity — a different map of what is bonded to what — makes them constitutional isomers. Butane and 2-methylpropane are both C4H10 but wired differently.
Same formula AND same connectivity, differing only in three-dimensional arrangement, makes them stereoisomers. This is the branch that needs care.

sections.heading: The trap: conformations are not isomers
body: Single bonds rotate freely at room temperature, millions of times a second. Two drawings of butane that differ only by rotation about a C−C bond are the same molecule caught in different poses, not two compounds.
The test is whether converting one into the other requires breaking a bond. If rotation alone does it, you have one compound.
Double bonds are the contrast: rotating one would tear the pi bond apart, which costs far too much energy. That is exactly why alkenes have cis and trans forms and alkanes do not.

sections.heading: Chirality and stereocenters
body: A carbon bonded to four DIFFERENT groups is a stereocenter, and its mirror image cannot be superimposed on the original — like left and right hands.
Check every group all the way out, not just the first atom. Two groups that both start with carbon can still differ further along.
Molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers, which includes every cis/trans pair.

example.label: Why this matters biologically
example.text: Enantiomers have identical melting points, boiling points and solubilities. They differ only toward other chiral things — and enzymes are chiral. That is why one enantiomer of a drug can be therapeutic while its mirror image does nothing.

sections.heading: Counting stereoisomers
body: With n stereocenters there are at most 2^n stereoisomers. Glucose has four, giving a family of sixteen — which is why sugar chemistry has so many named members.

The maximum is not always reached. If a molecule has an internal mirror plane it is superimposable on its own reflection and achiral despite having stereocenters. Those are meso compounds, and they are a favourite exam trap.

resonance.intro: Some molecules cannot be drawn correctly with a single Lewis structure. Resonance is the notation for that situation, and understanding what it does and does not claim prevents a specific misconception that causes trouble later.

sections.heading: What resonance actually says
body: When several valid Lewis structures differ only in where the electrons sit, the real molecule is none of them. It is a single, unchanging blend of all of them, called the hybrid.

The molecule does NOT flip between the structures. This is the misconception worth killing early. Benzene is not rapidly alternating between two arrangements of double bonds — it is permanently one thing, with all six carbon-carbon bonds identical and intermediate in length between a single and a double bond.
The double-headed arrow between structures means "is a blend of", not "turns into". An equilibrium arrow would mean something completely different: two real, separate species interconverting.

sections.heading: The one rule for drawing them
body: Only electrons move. Atoms stay exactly where they are. If you have moved an atom, you have drawn a different compound.

In practice the electrons move in a few recurring patterns: a lone pair swinging into a bond with an adjacent positive atom, a pi bond collapsing onto an adjacent atom as a lone pair, or a pi bond shifting one position along a conjugated chain.
It also requires geometry: the orbitals involved must be aligned so their p orbitals overlap side by side. Twist the system out of plane and the delocalization breaks.

example.label: Resonance versus tautomers
example.text: Two drawings of acetate differing in which C−O bond is double are resonance forms — only electrons moved. Two drawings where a hydrogen has relocated are tautomers: genuinely different compounds in equilibrium, written with an equilibrium arrow.

sections.heading: Not all structures contribute equally
body: When the possible structures are equivalent, they contribute equally and the charge is shared evenly. Acetate has two equivalent forms, so each oxygen carries exactly half a negative charge.
When they are not equivalent, the more stable one dominates. Rank them: full octets first, then fewest formal charges, then charges on sensible atoms (negative on electronegative ones).

sections.heading: Why delocalization stabilizes
body: Spreading charge over several atoms is lower in energy than concentrating it on one. That is the entire reason resonance matters for reactivity.

It is why carboxylic acids are millions of times more acidic than alcohols: the carboxylate spreads its negative charge over two oxygens while an alkoxide is stuck with it on one. The same logic explains why benzylic and allylic carbocations are unusually stable, and why the amide bond in proteins cannot rotate.

arrows.intro: Curved arrows are the language mechanisms are written in. They are not decoration on top of a reaction — they ARE the explanation, tracking where every electron goes. Learning to read them before mechanisms start in class removes most of the difficulty.

sections.heading: Arrows track electrons, nothing else
body: A curved arrow shows a pair of electrons moving from where they are now to where they end up. It never shows an atom moving.

The tail must start on actual electrons: either a lone pair or an existing bond. It never starts on an atom symbol, and never on a positive charge — a positive charge is where electrons are going TO, not coming from.
The head shows the destination. Landing between two atoms means a new bond forms there. Landing on a single atom means that atom keeps the pair as a lone pair.

sections.heading: Rich to poor, always
body: Electrons flow from electron-rich to electron-poor. The electron-rich species is the nucleophile — it has lone pairs, a negative charge, or an accessible pi bond. The electron-poor one is the electrophile: a positive charge, a partial positive, or an empty orbital.
This is why bond polarity matters so much. Identifying which carbon is δ+ tells you where the nucleophile will attack, and therefore where to point your arrow.
If you ever find yourself drawing an arrow that starts at a positive charge and points at something electron-rich, it is backwards.

sections.heading: Carbon can only hold four bonds
body: This constraint generates most of the two-arrow patterns you will draw. If a nucleophile forms a new bond to a carbon that already has four, something else must leave at the same time — so the attack arrow needs a partner arrow breaking a bond.
That is precisely why SN2 is a single concerted step with two arrows: the nucleophile comes in as the leaving group departs, and carbon is never five-bonded.

example.label: A quick self-check
example.text: After every step, verify three things: total charge is unchanged, no second-row atom exceeds an octet, and no carbon has five bonds. Almost every mechanism error shows up in one of those three.

sections.heading: Reading a mechanism from its arrows
body: The arrows tell you what kind of mechanism you have drawn. If a carbocation appears at any point, the pathway is stepwise — the leaving group departed before the nucleophile arrived. No intermediate means it was concerted.
That distinction has real consequences: a concerted backside attack inverts stereochemistry, while a flat carbocation can be attacked from either face and gives a mixture.

energy.intro: Two questions get asked about every reaction, and they are independent: is it favourable, and is it fast? Keeping them separate is one of the most useful habits you can build, because a reaction can be enormously favourable and still not happen at any observable rate.

sections.heading: Thermodynamics: is it favourable?
body: This is about where the reaction ends up, and it is answered by the free energy change, ΔG. Negative means products are lower in energy and favoured at equilibrium.
ΔG has two contributions: ΔH, the heat released or absorbed, and ΔS, the change in disorder, weighted by temperature. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

The temperature weighting is why heating a reaction can flip which product dominates. Elimination reactions produce more particles than substitution, so their ΔS is more positive, and raising T amplifies that advantage. "Heat favours elimination" is a consequence of this equation rather than a separate rule to memorize.

sections.heading: Kinetics: is it fast?
body: This is about the barrier in between, the activation energy Ea. Getting from reactants to products requires passing through a high-energy arrangement called the transition state, and Ea is the height of that climb.
Ea and ΔG are independent. Diamond converting to graphite is thermodynamically favourable and takes geological time, because the barrier is enormous.
A catalyst lowers Ea by offering a different route. It never changes ΔG or where the equilibrium sits — only how quickly you get there. Enzymes work exactly this way.

sections.heading: Reading a reaction coordinate diagram
body: Energy runs up the vertical axis and reaction progress along the horizontal. Every peak is a transition state and therefore one step, so counting peaks counts steps.
Every valley between two peaks is an intermediate: a real species with a genuine, if brief, lifetime. Carbocations live in these valleys. Transition states, sitting at maxima, can never be isolated.
The rate-determining step is the one with the tallest barrier measured from the valley BEFORE it — which is not always the highest point on the page.

example.label: A case where those differ
example.text: A profile running 0 → 60 → −30 → 50 → −40. The first peak (60) is higher on the page, but step two climbs from −30 up to 50, a rise of 80 against step one’s 60. Step two is rate-determining.

sections.heading: Why rate laws reveal mechanisms
body: Only species involved at or before the slow step can affect the rate. That makes the rate law experimental evidence for what the mechanism must be.

SN2 is second order — doubling either the substrate or the nucleophile doubles the rate — which tells you both are present in a single concerted step. SN1 is first order in substrate only, because the nucleophile joins after the slow ionization has already happened. The names literally encode this: the 1 and 2 are the molecularity of the rate-determining step.

biomolecules.intro: Biochemistry is organic chemistry applied to four families of molecule. The chemistry is the same chemistry — the same bonds, the same acid-base reasoning, the same intermolecular forces — assembled into larger structures with jobs to do.

sections.heading: Four families, one bond type each
body: Proteins are built from amino acids joined by peptide bonds, which are amides. Nucleic acids are nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds. Carbohydrates are sugars joined by glycosidic bonds. Fats are glycerol joined to fatty acids by ester bonds.

Three of those four are polymers built from repeating units. Lipids are the odd one out: they are grouped by a physical property, being insoluble in water, rather than by any shared backbone. That is why fats, steroids and phospholipids look so different from each other.
All four are assembled by condensation, releasing a water molecule per bond, and taken apart by hydrolysis, consuming one. Digestion is hydrolysis across all four families.

sections.heading: Protein structure in four levels
body: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids — just the order, nothing about shape.

Secondary structure is local folding into alpha helices and beta sheets, held together by hydrogen bonds between BACKBONE atoms. Side chains are not involved, which is why these patterns look the same regardless of sequence.

Tertiary structure is the whole chain folded into its three-dimensional shape, held by SIDE-CHAIN interactions. Quaternary structure is several separate chains assembled together, as in hemoglobin’s four subunits.

sections.heading: What actually drives folding
body: The dominant force is the hydrophobic effect, and the reason is counterintuitive: it is driven by WATER’s entropy, not the protein’s.

Water forced to surround a nonpolar group has to arrange itself into an ordered cage, which is entropically costly. Burying those nonpolar side chains in the protein’s core releases that structured water, and the resulting entropy gain drives folding.
So hydrophobic residues end up buried and polar ones face the water. In a membrane protein the logic inverts, because the surroundings are lipid rather than water.

example.label: The only covalent contribution
example.text: Everything holding tertiary structure together is non-covalent except one: two cysteine side chains can oxidize into a disulfide bridge. Denaturation destroys the fold while leaving the sequence intact, which is why a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.

sections.heading: Enzymes
body: Enzymes are proteins that catalyze reactions, and catalysis means exactly what it meant in kinetics: they lower the activation energy without changing ΔG or the equilibrium position.

They work by binding the substrate in a small pocket, the active site, and stabilizing the transition state. The residues doing the work are usually the ones with useful chemistry available: histidine shuttling protons, serine acting as a nucleophile, aspartate and glutamate stabilizing charge.
This is why enzymes have a pH optimum. Change the pH and you change the protonation state of those active-site residues, and the catalysis stops working.

orgopreview.intro: Substitution and elimination are the first big mechanism unit of the course, and they are where the foundations you have been building get used all at once. Seeing the shape of the problem now makes those weeks feel like a second exposure.

sections.heading: The situation
body: A carbon carries a leaving group — typically a halogen — which makes that carbon electron-poor. Something electron-rich arrives. There are two things it can do.

It can attack the carbon and replace the leaving group, which is SUBSTITUTION. Or it can act as a base, pull off a hydrogen from the neighbouring carbon, and form a double bond as the leaving group departs — ELIMINATION.
Each of those happens by two possible mechanisms, one concerted and one stepwise, giving four pathways: SN1, SN2, E1, E2. Predicting which one operates is the whole game.

sections.heading: Concerted versus stepwise
body: The 2 mechanisms happen in a single step. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group as it leaves, so carbon is never five-bonded — and that backside approach inverts the stereochemistry, like an umbrella in the wind.

The 1 mechanisms happen in two steps. The leaving group departs first, producing a carbocation, and only then does the nucleophile or base act. Because that carbocation is flat, it can be attacked from either face, giving a mixture of stereochemistry.
The digits are not arbitrary: they are the molecularity of the rate-determining step, which is why SN2 rate depends on both reagents and SN1 rate depends only on the substrate.

sections.heading: Deciding, in three questions
body: Ask the SUBSTRATE first, because it eliminates the most options fastest. Methyl and primary carbons cannot support a carbocation, so SN1 and E1 are out. Tertiary carbons are too crowded for backside attack, so SN2 is out. Secondary keeps everything open, and conditions decide.

Then ask about the REAGENT. A strong nucleophile drives SN2. A strong but bulky base — potassium tert-butoxide, LDA, DBU — cannot fit for backside attack, so it removes a proton instead and drives E2. A weak, neutral species, often the solvent itself, allows the slow ionization of SN1/E1.

Finally SOLVENT and TEMPERATURE break any remaining tie. Polar protic solvents stabilize ions and favour the stepwise routes; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile bare and reactive, favouring SN2. Heat favours elimination.

example.label: What this looks like in practice
example.text: 2-bromobutane with potassium tert-butoxide and heat. Secondary substrate settles nothing. But the base is strong AND bulky, which blocks SN2 and points at E2 — and the heat reinforces elimination. Answer: E2.

sections.heading: What to take from this now
body: You are not expected to be fluent in these yet. The point is that when the unit arrives, it should feel like assembling parts you already own rather than learning something new.

Every ingredient is something you have already met: carbocation stability from resonance and induction, leaving-group ability from acid-base reasoning, rate laws from kinetics, backside attack from three-dimensional geometry, and the entropy argument for heat from thermodynamics.
